#10622. What I had to unlearn when leaving a Fortune 500 company

For most of my corporate career, if an executive had a major speaking engagement in another country, someone from communications was getting on the plane. Often, that someone was me.

So when I moved to a startup and our CEO was invited to deliver a main-stage keynote in Paris, every instinct I’d built over more than a decade inside a Fortune 500 company told me what came next. Except this time, I didn’t get on the plane.

I worked closely on the narrative, the talk track, the slides, and coordinated with the conference team, right down to making sure his notes would appear on a downstage monitor. Then I sent him to Paris without me.

The talk was one of the strongest I’ve seen him deliver. Two years later, our team still references it and shares it with customers.

And that downstage monitor I’d carefully planned for? It wasn’t there. Something had gotten lost in translation. Fortunately, he didn’t need it.

4 THINGS I HAD TO UNLEARN

That moment captured something I’ve been learning as a leader: Becoming better can mean unlearning what doing the job well looked like.

The fundamentals I built over my career—storytelling, judgment, creativity, customer understanding, and trust—matter even more now. But some of the scaffolding around those fundamentals was built for another era. Here’s what I unlearned since.

1. Don’t rebuild the organization you left.

A startup gives you a blank canvas. That sounds freeing, until a major launch, when you notice every role that doesn’t exist. The instinct is to fill the boxes.

But I keep asking myself: If we were inventing this workflow today, would we build it the same way?

Increasingly, the answer is no.

I spent years building specialized expertise: shaping executive narratives, building thought-leadership platforms, and preparing leaders for high-stakes moments. At a startup, I’m experimenting with capturing that context in how we work, so others can use and adapt it.

The goal is to help expertise travel.

2. Don’t just make the old job faster. Redesign it.

Using AI to speed up one task is useful, but I’m more interested in what happens when teams start reimagining the work itself.

The questions I return to are simple. What context can we teach the system? Where is human judgment most important? How can someone use expertise that once lived in another person’s head?

I have a marketing team member who wanted to grow into communications. I started mentoring her on preparing executives for podcasts and speaking opportunities, and on building their social platforms. Instead of just teaching the skills, I shared how I train our brand and executive voices, so she could adapt them herself.

She went from learning to mapping out a full thought-leadership campaign on her own. After launch, an executive raved about her partnership. Soon she was building platforms for two more leaders, and bringing me ideas she’d dreamed up.

Democratizing expertise creates more builders. I’m learning to coach differently, giving others the context, tools, and confidence to build on what I know.

AI’s bigger opening is helping more people benefit from what each of us knows.

3. Speed is how fast you get it right.

Startup culture prizes speed. AI has sharpened that. Everyone expects instant answers. Recently I tested an AI workflow where the output took a few minutes. “It’s thinking,” the team said. The result was much closer to what I wanted than the usual instant response. I’d rather wait a few minutes than spend an hour prompting and rewriting.

The goal is getting it right, faster. And getting it right still requires people. That’s worth sitting with, because the pressure pulls the other way. When our team at Typeface surveyed 500+ marketing leaders, 62% admitted they’re already trading away quality, and 61% said the same about authenticity, to get cited by AI. Everyone is racing to be found. The first things to slip are the human signals that made a brand worth finding.

Being found is only the beginning. The advantage goes to brands that stay unmistakably themselves, whether they’re engaging a person or an AI agent. Human creativity is the differentiator that can’t be copied.

4. Being a strong leader doesn’t mean being in every room.

Back to Paris. I’d done the work, built the narrative, run the prep, developed the relationship. Something still went wrong, and the CEO was great.

My job was to help make sure he didn’t need me. I think about this with my team now. Sometimes an opportunity I would have owned before is better given to someone else. Sometimes expertise is more valuable when you teach it, or build it into a workflow others can use.

Scaling yourself is about creating impact in rooms you’re not in.

EXPERIENCE SHOULD GIVE YOU CONFIDENCE AND CURIOSITY

I left a Fortune 500 company for a startup expecting to be scrappy. Instead, I started questioning what we build with.

The way we work can be one thing. Context is another. The expertise of one person, captured and shared well, can serve many.

Maybe the most important one is our willingness to learn. AI is changing fast enough that none of us gets to be an expert forever. Our careers have given us judgment, pattern recognition, relationships, storytelling, and the ability to recognize great work. We also need a beginner’s mind to question the systems we’ve built around those skills.

Going first doesn’t mean adopting every new tool or discarding everything that came before. It means being willing to put your own assumptions on the table. Experience can be knowing what you’re willing to leave behind.

Courtney Brigham is senior director for communications and brand at Typeface.

#10621. How to Get a YouTube API Key and Use the Data API (2026)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You need a YouTube API key the moment your app has to read anything from YouTube: a video's length, its view count, a channel's latest uploads. Getting one takes about five minutes. Using it well takes a little longer, because YouTube changed how its quota works in June 2026, and plenty of guides still describe the old rules.

In this guide we'll get a key, lock it down and test it. Then we'll use it from Node.js for three real jobs: adding up the length of a playlist, listing a channel's videos without spending a search, and estimating what a video earned. Along the way we'll cover what the YouTube API costs (nothing), how the 2026 quota works, and the errors you're most likely to hit.

A YouTube API key identifies your project to the YouTube Data API v3. With just a key, you can read public data:

A key isn't enough for anything that touches someone's account. Uploading videos, editing playlists or reading private data needs OAuth 2.0, where the user signs in and grants your app access.

You'll need a Google account. The YouTube Data API is free, so there's nothing to pay for.

The restrictions matter more than they look. A key is just a string in a URL, and anyone who copies an unrestricted one can spend your daily quota for you. With an API restriction, the key is useless for other Google APIs. With an application restriction, it only works from your server or your site. Changes to restrictions can take up to five minutes to apply, so don't panic if a request fails straight after you save.

Before writing any code, check the key with a single request. This one asks for the first video ever uploaded to YouTube, and uses the fields parameter to trim the response down to four values:

That request cost 1 unit of your daily quota, which brings us to the question everyone asks.

Yes. There's no charge per request and no paid plan. Instead you get a daily quota, and since June 1, 2026 it's split into separate buckets:

Google's quota calculator lists the cost of every method. Quotas reset at midnight Pacific Time. Every request costs at least 1 unit, including requests that fail, so a retry loop around a broken call can use up a day's quota on its own.

If you've read older guides, search is the big change. A search used to cost 100 units out of the same 10,000, so 100 searches emptied your whole day. Uploads were worse still, at about 1,600 units each until December 2025. Now both have their own buckets, and the 10,000 units are left for everything else.

To give you a feel for what 10,000 units buys, here's what each example in this guide costs:

You can't pay for more. To go above the defaults, fill in the YouTube API Services Audit and Quota Extension Form, which is linked from Google's page on quota and compliance audits. YouTube first audits your project to check it follows the YouTube API Services Terms of Service, then someone from the API team gets back to you. Google doesn't give a timeline, so apply well before you need the extra quota.

Most projects never need to. The rest of this guide is about getting a lot done with very few units.

The examples need Node.js 20.6 or later, for the built-in fetch and the --env-file flag. There are no packages to install. Make a folder with a .env file in it:

Every example imports one small helper. It builds the URL, adds your key and turns API errors into readable messages:

Run any example with node --env-file=.env followed by the file name.

YouTube doesn't tell you how long a playlist is. To work it out, you need two methods:

Durations come back in ISO 8601 format. PT15M33S is 15 minutes 33 seconds, PT1H2M3S adds an hour, and a stream longer than a day looks like P1DT2H3M4S. The toSeconds() function below handles all three.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Full Courses in One Video playlist:

That's 184 hours of courses for 4 units of quota. Private and deleted videos still show up in a playlist's items, but videos.list doesn't return them, which is why the script prints "52 of 52 videos available". On a playlist with removed videos, the two numbers will differ.

This is the core of the free YouTube playlist length calculator I built on createthat.ai. The live version adds a target time box that works out the speed you need to finish by a deadline, and it accepts channel, video and Shorts links as well as playlists.

The obvious way to find a channel's videos is to search for them. Don't: search is now capped at 100 calls a day, and it isn't built to list everything a channel has posted. Every channel has an uploads playlist instead, and you can reach it in two cheap calls:

Two units, and none of your 100 daily searches. To get every upload rather than the newest five, page through the playlist with the same pageToken loop as Example 1.

videos.list with part=statistics returns a video's view, like and comment counts. Dislike counts have been private since December 2021 and favoriteCount is always 0, so don't build anything on those. The script also copes with a missing like or comment count, which you'll see on some videos.

This time the fields parameter trims the response to the values we use. That makes the response smaller, but it doesn't change the cost: the call is 1 unit either way.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Learn Python full course, one of the most-watched videos in that playlist:

Treat the last line as a rough range, not an answer. The Data API doesn't share anyone's revenue, so any estimate is views multiplied by an RPM: what a creator keeps per 1,000 views. RPM moves a lot with the topic and where the viewers live, and the estimate assumes the video shows ads, which not every channel does.

And sometimes you don't need an API at all. When I built a font tester, I needed a list of Google Fonts. The Google Fonts Developer API would have meant a key and a call on every visit, for a list that barely changes. Instead I generated a file of the 500 most popular fonts once, from Google's public font metadata, and the page loads it like any other file. No key, no quota and nothing to fail.

When a call fails, the response's error.message and error.details[0].reason tell you why. These are the ones you'll see most:

For the invalid key error, the full response looks like this:

Yes. Creating a key and calling the YouTube Data API costs nothing. You're limited by the daily quota instead, and there's no paid tier: more quota comes through an audit.

In the Google Cloud console, select your project and go to APIs & Services > Credentials. Your keys are listed under API keys, with a Show key option next to each one.

It works, but anyone can read the key from your page. If you do it, restrict the key to your website and to the YouTube Data API v3. A small server route that calls the API for you is safer, and it gives you somewhere to cache results.

By default, 100 searches, 100 uploads and 10,000 units for everything else. Most reads cost 1 unit and videos.list takes 50 IDs per call, so that's enough for the details of up to 500,000 videos a day.

Getting a YouTube API key is the easy part: one project, one API to enable, one key and two restrictions. The 2026 quota is generous if you work with it:

All three examples together cost 7 units, out of 10,000. From here, try commentThreads.list to pull a video's comments 100 at a time, or extend Example 2 to page through a channel's entire upload history and add it all up with the code from Example 1.

12V-2x6 strikes again, but thankfully it didn't take out a GPU this time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Reddit user u/Doomslayer606 posted about frayed braided sleeving on both 12V-2x6 cables for their two RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation GPUs the other day, asking whether it’s normal cable degradation or a sign of overheating. The GPUs were running at 500W, below the maximum 600W power draw, but commenters are confident it’s overheated cables, as the poster reports stiff, cracked, and easily peeling sleeves on only some of the wires.

u/Doomslayer606 posted on r/PcBuild with the title “Did I just save my RTX PRO 6000 GPUs from melting?” with photos of the 12V-2x6 cable’s braided sleeving frayed. The poster asked in the description whether this was normal degradation, a manufacturing issue, or overheating. The poster reported that the damaged braided sleeving felt stiff and peeled off easily, which is a strong indication of heat damage, and the comments were sure that it was.

Luckily, the poster’s GPUs were safe, but the 12-2x6 connectors are notorious for melting due to high power draw. One comment asked if they kept the stock power limit, to which the poster responded that they lowered both GPUs to 500W — another user responded asking why the poster wouldn’t use 300W, but the poster said it would reduce performance by up to 50% and they need to keep up with their deadlines.

Theoretically, the cable should be able to handle 500W, as each positive pin would only handle 6.94 A, which isn’t enough current to significantly heat up 16 AWG wire, but one of the main causes of cable overheating is uneven current distribution across the pins. Since only two of the pins melted on both cables, it’s likely those received high-current spikes often, leading to heat buildup.

Users have suggested aftermarket cables like the Corsair ThermalProtect 12V-2x6 cable that detects overheating cables, and the Thermal Grizzly WireView Pro II or Aqua Computing AMPINEL, which have active current balancing to prevent any wire from taking too much current alone. In a recent story, someone even created a power distributor, distributing the 12 pins into two 8-pin cables with a custom-designed PCB, which lowered the cable temperatures significantly — while another modder had a cursed solution, soldering thick cables directly to the RTX 5090’s power pins.

In an ideal world, consumers shouldn’t need another product or mod their GPUs to stop them destroying themselves. GPUs have only gotten more powerful, but instead of using more or thicker wires, we’re getting fewer wires of the same thickness. Understandably, having multiple 8-pin connectors gets messy, but surely there has to be a better solution. Maybe GPUs have outgrown the Mini-Fit Jr. connectors and need to have their own special connector with thicker pins and thicker wires.

#10618. How to drive social impact and business value together

Companies are often asked to drive business value while simultaneously supporting their communities. In my experience, both goals can be accomplished at the same time. We see it happening in multiple industries.

HP, for example, has connected its social impact efforts directly to its mission of helping people succeed through technology. Through its Future of Work Accelerator, the company supports nonprofits that expand access to digital tools, workforce training, and economic opportunity. The initiative helps more people develop the skills needed in today’s economy while strengthening the broader ecosystem of future workers and entrepreneurs, as well as technology users.

FedEx has taken a similar approach through its Entrepreneur Fund and Boost Camp. Small businesses make up a significant portion of the company’s customer base, and the program provides entrepreneurs with funding, mentorship, and business training to help them grow and scale their ventures. In doing so, FedEx supports local economic growth and job creation, along with small business success. At the same time, FedEx helps bolster the network of businesses that rely on its shipping and logistics services.

These efforts share a common thread: They create programs that benefit individuals and communities in need while advancing company goals.

OUR APPROACH

As NBC celebrates its 100th anniversary this year, we also have an opportunity to make a difference. We challenged ourselves to come up with an innovative way to honor our legacy while investing in the future of the creative industry.

As a media and entertainment company, our social impact efforts are naturally focused on helping the next generation of storytellers build skills, gain meaningful experience, and develop their craft.

That legacy shaped the Power of Storytelling Grants program, developed in partnership with The Alliance for Media Arts + Culture. We selected 10 emerging producers to receive $5,000 grants to create an original 30-second promotional spot honoring NBC’s centennial milestone. Each project drew from the broadcast network’s rich archive, using our iconic intellectual property to recognize our innovation, cultural moments, and industry firsts while fostering the growth of emerging creatives. One winner’s promo was selected to run across Comcast NBCUniversal platforms as part of the company’s anniversary celebration, which culminates in an on-air NBC special on December 10th.

Importantly, the grant recipients also received editorial guidance and mentorship from employee volunteers throughout the process. Access to advisors, professional networks, and real-world assignments can be the difference between aspiring to a dream job and building the key skills that will put a young creator on the path to attaining it.

The participants selected for this program were sourced from nonprofit media arts organizations, including Kids in the Spotlight, New Orleans Video Access Center, PhillyCAM, Reel Works, RE:IMAGINE, and Youth FX. These organizations are helping cultivate creative talent across the country through paid apprenticeships, and our grant program provided them with a rare opportunity for a masterclass in editing with archival footage.

INVEST IN THE NEXT GENERATION

For the winning filmmaker, Danya Granado, the experience represented more than a typical creative assignment. It was a rare moment to engage directly with a century of iconic content and cultural history. As she puts it, “The NBCU archive represents a hundred years of how people have seen news, entertainment, and each other. Getting direct access to that material feels like an invitation to be in conversation with that legacy.”

Stories like Danya’s underscore the value of capitalizing on a company’s greatest assets to invest in the next generation of talent.

Across industries, companies are creating programs that broaden access and strengthen communities. They address real societal needs while also advancing business goals. Whether it’s storytelling, technology, sports, innovation, or another core capability, every business has a superpower. The key is to use it in ways that open doors and create pathways. It should solve real challenges while also advancing strategic objectives.

Yes, it’s community impact. It’s also smart business. When done well, it’s exactly what corporate social responsibility should be: a win-win for the community and the company.

Hilary Smith is executive vice president of corporate social responsibility at NBCUniversal.

#10617. Google Messages homepage redesign: Pinned chat avatars, bottom search, corner Gemini

In addition to the new app icon, Google Messages for Android is testing a big homepage redesign that has three core components.

Update 11/7: Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.

This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s currently just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.

You’ll see large contact photos appear above all chats, which pushes the list of other conversations down the page. Like iMessage on iOS, this layout has the downside of not showing any history or last sent information.

Meanwhile, Google is testing another change where search becomes a centered floating action button (FAB) alongside new chat. When you’re scrolling down the page, you’ll see “Search” in a pill-shaped button, with the other button minimized.

Hate the idea of just the pinned "bobble head" look. I like being able to view message tidbits. Plus, it's directly copying Apple (enough said). I have to use an iPhone at my job. I hate the pinned bubble conversation look and more importantly it's function.

Otherwise, you’ll see a circular magnifying glass icon and “Start chat” in the pill. The animation that accompanies this change looks nice and feels alive, while boosting one-handed usability.

Google has replaced the Gemini FAB with a button in the top-right corner next to your profile image. This matches the design leveraged by Workspace apps on desktop and mobile.

These updates are currently in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to all testers. Some users have all aspects of the redesign, but it appears that Google is rolling out the various components in a piecemeal fashion.

#10615. PepsiCo layoffs: 1,000 jobs reportedly slashed as CEO pushes soda giant to ‘be faster’ and ‘more capable’

November has already been a tough month for layoffs.

In the tech sector, numerous big-name companies, including Amazon, Block, and Squarespace, have already cut roles or are planning to. But workplace reductions are not limited to just tech.

Yesterday, soft drink giant PepsiCo, Inc. (Nasdaq: PEP) reportedly announced that it will lay off around 1,000 employees in North America as sales in the region underperform. Here’s what you need to know.

Pepsi tells employees to prepare for job cuts

PepsiCo CEO Ram Krishnan wrote to employees stating that the company will cut around 1,000 positions in North America in the coming days, multiple media outlets reported.

In the email Krishnan sent to employees (per CNBC), the Pepsi boss said the company’s ambitions were to “build a stronger, more future-fit business that delivers industry-leading growth” in North America.

He added: “To do that, we need to be faster, more connected, and more capable, while continuing to invest in growth — behind our people, capabilities and brands.”

Unfortunately, the endeavor also involves layoffs.

“We will simplify how we operate, better connect teams and strengthen the capabilities we need,” Krishnan wrote. “The goal is to move faster, execute better and invest behind the opportunities that will drive our growth.” The Wall Street Journal first reported the layoffs.

The layoffs will be limited to Pepsi’s North American workforce, which includes roughly 125,000 positions in the United States.

Worldwide, Pepsi employs about 306,000 people as of the end of last year. The layoffs will reportedly happen over the coming week.

Fast Company reached out to PepsiCo for comment.

Pepsi’s North American sales lag other global markets

Last month, Pepsi announced its Q3 2026 financial results, which were broadly respectable. Net revenue increased 5.6%, and operating profit increased 19%.

As CNBC reported at the time, the company’s $25.27 billion in revenue for the quarter exceeded street expectations of $24.96 billion, and its adjusted EPS of $2.34 exceeded the $2.29 analysts had expected.

But Pepsi’s relatively positive results largely came from its international markets, which, year-to-date, have accounted for 41% of its net revenue.

In Pepsi’s home territory of North America, things are less rosy.

The North American food division of Pepsi, which includes products like Frito-Lay snacks, saw volume remain flat, while its beverage business volume declined by 2%.

The lackluster results in North America led Pepsi to reduce its core earnings per share expectations for the full 2026 fiscal year. Previously, Pepsi had expected growth of 5% to 7%. Now it expects growth of 2.5% to 3.5%.

When it came to Pepsi’s North American snacks results, the company blamed the lackluster demand on “the consumer environment.”

Pepsi stock loses its fizz

Pepsi’s North American numbers are the only thing going flat. The company’s share price has lost its fizz over the course of 2026. 

PEP stock began the year performing strongly: By late February, shares were up over 20% since the year began. But since a high above $170 reached in early 2026, Pepsi shares have declined significantly. 

As of yesterday’s close, PEP stock traded at $141. While its share price has increased more than 12% over the past 30 days, that recovery has not been enough to erase the mid-year losses.

As of yesterday’s close, PEP shares were down 1.1% for the year. The broader S&P 500 is up more than 10% over that same period.

But if Pepsi executives hoped layoffs could quickly boost the company’s stock price, they’ll be disappointed. While investors tend to cheer layoffs, since cutting jobs is often the easiest way to quickly improve the bottom line, they seem to have shrugged off the news.

Since the job cuts became public yesterday, PEP shares have hardly moved. Yesterday, Pepsi stock closed up just under four-tenths of a percent, and today in premarket trading, shares are up about the same amount as of the time of this writing.

#10614. Android tablets are back, but are they for you?

Android tablets have always been a bit of a touchy subject, but it’s abundantly clear that the form factor is making a comeback. But, as someone who’s a fan of the smaller sizes, are you actually using the gargantuan Android tablets that every company seems obsessed with? In other words – are you the customer for the Android tablets these brands are selling?

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

For a while there, Android tablets had hit what felt like a dead end. Bigger smartphones and cooling of the tablet market as a whole, along with the general sentiment that Apple was doing a way better job with the iPad anyway, left the category in a place that felt stagnant – and that’s the nice way of putting it.

But, over the past few years, Android tablets have had a renaissance.

New form factors, big releases from a variety of brands, and flagship-tier devices left and right. Despite Android’s push into foldables and still-huge displays on nearly every smartphone, tablets are very much back. Prior to RAMageddon’s worst impacts, tablet sales were growing for nearly everyone, and Android brands were seeing a larger slice of the pie.

Anyway, this is on my mind right now because I’ve had a lot of Android tablets arrive in my office in the past few weeks, capping off a lot of tablet announcements in the past few months. I just finished up with Redmagic Astra 2, a tablet I think fits the description of “Android’s iPad Mini OLED,” and I’m in the process of moving into tablets from Lenovo and Amazon. Our Jordan Floyd has also been testing out the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra behind the scenes. And if there’s one trend amongst recent tablet releases, it’s that big tablets seem to be the primary focus among a lot of brands.

Take Amazon’s new Google Play-equipped Alexa Tablet lineup, for example.

The Alexa Tablet 12 is the crown jewel of the lineup, packing the most powerful specs and a premium anti-glare display. It’s the only one that gets a “Pro” moniker, while the 11-inch and 8-inch models are noticeable steps down. Unboxing the Alexa Tablet 8 this week, for example, I was immediately reminded this is not a premium device – the screen makes that clear without any hesitation whatsoever. It was a case of whiplash after setting up the Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 with its 4K display.

It’s a weird one for me. I’ve never been a big fan of these super-sized Android tablets (or iPads, for that matter). I can get behind a 10-inch or 11-inch model, but I find myself more at home on the smaller slates. They’re fantastic for travel as an alternative to draining my phone’s battery, while I find myself just reaching for a laptop instead if I want a bigger screen. A big tablet, regardless of specs, can rarely replace a proper laptop for me, so lugging both around just sounds like more trouble than it’s worth.

But, clearly, people are buying these bigger slates. Samsung appears to be seeing enough success with its mammoth Galaxy Tab S Ultra lineup to keep the 14.6-inch tablet around each year while the smaller sizes are now on an every-other-year cycle. Lenovo’s lineup is virtually all underpowered when the screen size goes down, aside from the Legion Tab that’s now $900.

Are you buying these bigger tablets? What are you using them for?

I imagine that most folks opting for a bigger tablet are using these in the place of a laptop. Thinner and lighter, longer battery life, etc. And in cases like the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro and its $550~ price tag, I get the appeal. Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 takes that down a notch for me at $799 – you’re getting into laptop territory there – but it still is a compelling-enough alternative if it fits your needs. The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra at $1,400 plus a $200 keyboard, yeah I don’t get that one at all.

Let’s discuss! I want to know if you’re using an Android tablet, what you’re using it for, and what size you actually prefer.

Ladies and gents, we’ve finally got a new flagship in the US. Motorola Signature 27 is launching on November 19 and looks excellent, though its flashy spec sheet won’t come cheap at $1,599.

Finally, something good came out of Googlebook

Googlebook is a disaster, but there’s finally one good thing coming out of it in Henry Cavill’s new “Mustache Protocol” game which, supposedly, was built on Googlebook. I’ll bite my tongue there, but the accompanying video brought a needed bit of joy into my week.

I use an 8" Samsung. Not the best in specs, but fine for browsing and reading books. I had a Nexus 10 years ago and gave it to my sister-in-law as I rarely needed something that big. My wife also uses an 8" Samsung, mostly for reading.

#10613. Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Review: Slim OLED gaming that doesn't last long

The Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI mostly succeeds as a thin-and-light gaming laptop, offering solid RTX 5070 Ti performance, a beautiful 240 Hz OLED display, comfortable input devices, and plentiful ports. Its biggest weakness is ironically its battery life, which falls short of what you'd expect from a system focused on portability.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Not everyone wants a hulking gaming laptop. Some prefer something stealthier. Acer’s Predator Helios Neo 16S AI aims for portability but still packs a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor and Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics into a sub-five-pound package. It also includes plenty of ports and a beautiful 240 Hz OLED display. That hardware gives it plenty to work with, but the question remains whether the Helios Neo 16S AI can still deliver solid gaming performance while being portable.

Acer’s obsidian black chassis maintains the look of the Predator series – angular, dark, and visible in the dark with its illuminated lid logo. At 14.05 x 10.85 x 0.74 inches and 4.85 pounds, it’s respectably trim for a gaming laptop, though the Gigabyte Aero X16 (14 x 9.9 x 0.78 inches, 4.2 pounds) and the HyperX Omen 15 (13.5 x 9.96 x 0.93 inches, 4.89 pounds) both have about an inch less depth since neither use a rear thermal shelf like Acer.

The build quality is decent – both the chassis and lid show little flex. The stamped aluminum panels on the lid bottom and chassis lid aren’t ultra-premium but still beat plastic. One downside is that the metal shows fingerprints easily, which are difficult to clean off.

Acer provides an impressive port variety across three sides: Thunderbolt 4, three USB-A 3.2, USB-C 3.2, HDMI 2.1, 2.5 Gbps Ethernet, a MicroSD card reader, and an audio jack. The rear ports conveniently leave cables out of sight.

Inside, the laptop offers Wi-Fi 6E, which isn’t as modern as it could be, though the Killer AX1675i card and accompanying Killer Ethernet jack offer simultaneous network connections via Killer Doubleshot Pro for gamers that want to ensure network priority for the games over one connection and all other apps over the other. It’s also notable that Acer includes a zippered, padded travel sleeve.

Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti (12GB GDDR7, 1,612 MHz boost clock, 115 W maximum graphics power)

16-inch, OLED, 16:10, 2560 x 1600, 240 Hz, G-Sync

Thunderbolt 4, 3x USB-A 3.2, USB-C 3.2, HDMI 2.1, Ethernet, MicroSD card reader, audio

14.05 x 10.85 x 0.74 inches (357 x 276 x 18.8 mm)

We tested the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI with a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor, Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics card, and 16GB of RAM.

Playing 007 First Light, I saw about 65 to 75 frames per second (FPS) in most scenes, with spikes to over 100 FPS in wide open areas. The game remained all-around playable, though it did require using DLSS to achieve these framerates at native 2560 x 1600 with High settings.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Our comparison systems for this Acer are Gigabyte’s Aero X16 (Ryzen AI 7 350, RTX 5070 85W, $1,899.99 when tested, $1,499.99 as of this writing) and HyperX’s Omen 15 (Core Ultra 9 386H, RTX 5070 85W, $2,099.99 when tested, about $3,159.99 as of this writing).

Comparisons will focus on the 1920 x 1080 results, but we also included numbers at each laptop’s native resolution: 2560 x 1600 for the Acer and Gigabyte while the HP uses 2880 x 1800.

Overall, the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI performed significantly better than both the Gigabyte and HyperX laptops. Much of that has to do with its higher-wattage RTX 5070 Ti, though its Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor is also more modern.

In Shadow of the Tomb Raider (Highest detail preset), Acer’s 125 FPS at 1080p was on par with the HyperX (126 FPS), though it dominated at its 1600p native resolution, with 76 FPS against Gigabyte’s 60 FPS and HyperX’s 64 FPS.

Acer’s advantage continued in Far Cry 6 (Ultra), where it produced 122 FPS to Gigabyte’s 85 FPS and HyperX’s 107 FPS at native resolution. The lead narrowed in Red Dead Redemption 2 (Medium) where Acer and Gigabyte practically tied at 1080p and were within a few FPS at native (52 FPS for Acer and 49 FPS for Gigabyte). The HyperX remained behind.

The Acer also demonstrated markedly better performance in Cyberpunk 2077 (Ray Tracing Ultra) particularly at native resolution, where its 21 FPS outran Gigabyte (17 FPS) and HyperX (5 FPS).

In Forza Horizon 6 (Extreme), Acer’s 72 FPS at 1080p was strangely lower than HyperX’s 80 FPS, but the results flipped at native, where Acer’s 60 FPS was considerably ahead of HyperX’s 51 FPS.

While not a powerhouse, the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI demonstrates competent gaming performance at its 2560 x 1600 native resolution. Crucially, the extra depth from Acer’s thermal shelf design lets its GPU draw 115 W, considerably more than its Gigabyte and HyperX competitors

We test the sustained performance of gaming laptops running 15 loops of the Metro: Exodus stress test, simulating half an hour of gaming. During the test, the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI averaged 86.82 FPS across all runs. The variance was less than one FPS between runs, indicating stable thermal performance. The Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus ran at an average of 2.94 GHz on its P-cores, 2.16 GHz on its E-cores, and had an average temperature of 73 degrees Celsius. Meanwhile, the RTX 5070 Ti averaged 1.622 GHz and 74 C.

Our Predator Helios Neo 16S AI features a Core Ultra 9 290HX processor, 16GB of dual-channel DDR5-6400 memory, and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD.

The Acer’s Core Ultra 9 290HX produced strong numbers in Geekbench. Its single-core score of 3,349 and multi-core score of 19,313 were well ahead of the Ryzen AI 7 350-powered Gigabyte (2,916 and 14,074) and Core Ultra 9 386H-powered HyperX (2,857 and 15,916). This continued into our 4K-to-1080p Handbrake transcoding testing, which Acer dominated with 2 minutes and 30 seconds. The Gigabyte (3:54) and HyperX (3:39) weren’t even close.

Acer also produced solid numbers in our 25GB file transfer test, averaging 2,034.84 MBps next to Gigabyte’s1,480.57 MBps and HyperX’s far slower 999.57 MBps.

Overall, this Acer is very capable for almost any kind of use. Multitasking will be limited by 16GB of RAM, but Acer sells versions of this laptop with 32GB and it can be upgraded after purchase.

Once glance at this Acer’s display leaves no doubt it’s a key selling point. Its OLED panel technology creates exceptionally vivid colors matched by excellent brightness, and its glossy surface gives it an almost liquid appearance. The 2560 x 1600 resolution is a good balance between detail and what the system’s RTX 5070 Ti graphics card can drive in today’s games. Gamers will also appreciate the smooth 240 Hz refresh rate and Nvidia G-Sync support. (As we’ll see in the battery life section, the screen only supports 240 Hz, resulting in higher-than-expected power consumption.)

Watching nature documentaries on National Geographic, I noted the vibrant colors of tropical scenes and the pitch blacks of the depths of the sea. Gaming was equally immersive – 007 First Light felt supremely fluid and looked sharp. I could even make out the writing on character’s uniform badges without zooming.

The Acer’s display covered a healthy 82.7% of the DCI-P3 color gamut, matching the Gigabyte, although it wasn’t quite in the same league as the HyperX, which also used an OLED panel. It also didn’t match the HyperX in brightness, but with a peak of 372.4 nits in SDR, the Acer boasts solid brightness for OLED. Our 40% HDR testing revealed up to an impressive 608 nits of brightness.

Acer’s keyboard offers a satisfying feel, with ample throw and cushioning without feeling rubbery. In MonkeyType, I reached 116 words per minute with 99% accuracy on my first try, a great result for me on any laptop. The Acer Key app lets you customize the user-customizable key above the plus key, which is handy for creating one-press access to a favorite app or site.

Though the keyboard doesn't feature per-key backlighting, its four RGB zones can be set to many patterns and colors in the PredatorSense app. When changing lighting settings, the app initially says they’re controlled by Windows Dynamic Lighting, but that isn’t the case since Dynamic Lighting says no compatible devices are detected. But once dismissing the warning in PredatorSense, the app provides intuitive if limited control over the zones and lid logo. Each zone can be assigned a static lighting effect or the entire keyboard set in a dynamic pattern: breathing, neon, wave, ripple, combo, snake, and disco, with customizable speed, direction, and brightness. Settings can be stored in profiles.

Acer also did well with the large touchpad, which offers predictable clicking and my fingers glided smoothly over the matte surface.

Audio performance isn’t a strong point for the Neo 16S AI. Twin speakers embedded in the palm rest barely have enough volume for casual listening, with average clarity and thin bass. In Phil Collins’ “Don’t Lose My Number”, drum hits sounded flat and vocals were somewhat muted.

The speakers are better-suited gaming, offering a decent sense of direction because of their placement on either side of the palm rest, but lack of bass and volume means you'll want a headset. The DTS:X app offers equalizers – without them, the sound is quite tinny. I had the best results leaving the equalizer on Auto.

With ten Torx T6 screws securing the bottom cover, Acer doesn’t make it easy to get inside the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI. Removing the screws is the easy part – finding an entry point for my plastic pry tool provided harder. I eventually found one at the front corners of the chassis by using mild force. The fact that the side vents are part of the bottom cover compounds the difficulty – I needed to find an opening for my pry tool above those as well. The clips made cringeworthy snapping sounds as they were released, though surprisingly, none cracked off.

The effort is not for naught – Acer offers solid upgradeability, with two SODIMM slots under the black plastic cover in the middle, plus an M.2 2280 SSD slot and M.2 2230 wireless card slot. The battery is also replaceable.

Our battery testing consists of web browsing, running OpenGL tests, and streaming videos with the screen at 150 nits while connected to Wi-Fi. The Predator underwhelmed here despite having a large 92 WHr battery – the HyperX laptop outlasted it by almost two hours and the Gigabyte nearly two and a half hours. Most of the blame goes to Acer’s decision to use a screen locked at 240 Hz; more advanced displays would support a variable refresh rate or at least allow it to be lowered to 60 Hz.

We measure laptop surface temperatures during 15 loops of the Metro: Exodus stress test. During the test, the Acer’s temperatures peaked at 103 degrees F between the keyboard G and H keys, 81 F on the touchpad, and a toasty 129 F on bottom-center. Fan noise is audible particularly while gaming; hearing softer sounds in games will require using a headset. For daily use, the laptop hardly makes any noise.

PredatorSense remains the prominent app on Acer’s Predator gaming laptops. On the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI, it offers power settings, system monitoring, updates, and system settings. Power profiles include quiet, balanced (the default), performance, and turbo. Performance mode indicates it overclocks the CPU and GPU, but doesn’t specify details, while turbo appears to be performance mode but with the fan speeds maxed.

The app’s settings let you disable Nvidia Optimus, set up optimized battery charging, a bluelight shield, and toggle a 30-second keyboard backlighting timeout. Fan control is possible, though the custom option only allows you to set the RPM, not a curve. Most of the settings above plus lighting effects and a sound equalizer can be saved in scenario profiles.

Acer loads many more apps than PredatorSense – too many: Acer Assist, Acer Chroma Tune, Acer Intelligence Space, Acer LiveArt, Acer documents, Acer Jumpstart, Acer Legal Information, Acer My Key, Acer Purified Voice Console, Acer PurifiedView, and Acer QuickPanel create a lengthy list under the Start Menu’s “A” section. Many of them are simply links to the Windows Store.

Some of the apps actually installed are useful, like Acer My Key mentioned earlier. Others could be: Acer Intelligence Space provides many AI-driven features like a meeting assistant, an image generator, a media search tool, and a game assistant that claims to automatically change the color of your crosshair for maximum visibility. I didn’t test all these out – they aren’t specific to the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI – but it seems that they could add value if you’re not already vested in other AI services.

There’s also a decent amount of bloatware, including a McAfee trial, a Dropbox promotion, and Forge of Empires. While easily uninstalled, they simply don’t belong on a laptop this expensive.

Our Predator Helios Neo 16S AI includes a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus CPU, Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics card, 16GB of dual-channel RAM, a 1TB PCIe 4.0 solid-state drive, and a 16-inch 2560 x 1600 OLED display with a 240 Hz refresh rate. It retails for $2,774.99 from Best Buy, though I did see it briefly drop to $1,999.99 during my review period.

Best Buy also offers a 32GB version for $3,199.99, but it was discounted to $2,459.99 during our review period, making it less expensive than our model. Pricing is always in flux with the ongoing memory shortages, but Acer’s list prices are in line with market expectations. At Best Buy, many RTX 5070 Ti models hover around the same price as our model and many are pricier.

Acer also lists a $2,099.99 model on its site with 16GB of RAM, a 1TB SSD, and an RTX 5060, though I didn’t find this model for sale.

The Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI delivers on most of its thin-and-light gaming promise. Its RTX 5070 Ti provides solid gaming performance on its beautiful 240 Hz OLED display, and it follows up with a comfortable keyboard and touchpad, useful port selection, and solid upgradeability.

The trouble is that its portability is undermined by its below average battery life, an ironic shortcoming for a thin-and-light laptop. Audible gaming fans and lackluster speakers are further compromises, but the limited unplugged runtime is the one that those seeking a more portable package ought to be most concerned about.

But if you’re after a relatively slim gaming laptop to take between places where you can plug in, the Helios Neo 16S AI is an otherwise appealing package.

Charles Jefferies is a freelance reviewer for Tom’s Hardware US. He covers laptop and desktop PCs, especially gaming models.

#10612. Paige Paul’s world of Dairy Boy is collabing with Hanes and coming to Target

Before the lifestyle brand Dairy Boy had a logo or a single follower, Paige Paul—formerly Paige Lorenze—was a New School student crafting a mood board made up of vlogs and pictures.

In 2021, that vision became the Dairy Boy brand—a name inspired by Paul’s love of dairy products like whole milk, which, in the age of oat milk lattes, seemed radical.

Paul, who now has an audience of more than 2.3 million across platforms, filled the brand with products that showcase pieces of her life. Her upbringing on the East Coast and the changing seasons translate into white eyelet cotton dresses in the summer and colorful fleece jackets in the winter. Then there’s the Instagram-ready pajama sets, and a sporty drop just in time for a US Open run by her husband, the American tennis player Tommy Paul. (He made it as far as the Round of 16 this year.)

“Before I had a brand, I feel like I was building a world,” Paige Paul tells Fast Company.

Now, that world of patterns and Americana lore is growing past the sold-out drops and pop-ups with hour-long lines. Dairy Boy is partnering on a limited-edition collaboration with Hanes that will sell online and at more than 1,200 Target stores nationwide beginning November 14.

Dairy Boy’s first major collaboration since it launched five years ago pairs Paul’s Americana dream with a staple of that fantasy: a brand built on comfort and functionality just like hers, but rooted in basics that were lacking in her existing collections.

“Everyone in my life, male or woman, has owned something from Hanes, and I think that is what true heritage legacy brand means in America,” Paul says. “Dairy Boy’s collections are so often vibrant and specific, and I felt like the basic side of our business is something that deserved doing it with the best in class.”

Working alongside Hanes and Target allowed Paul to keep pricing affordable. That’s a priority she traced to her days at the New School, the lower Manhattan parent of the Parsons School of Design and other colleges, when she was looking for a price point she could afford while in college.

The collection keeps the cuts, fabrics, and silhouettes of original Hanes styles, but reimages them through the lens of Dairy Boy. For instance, the collection pairs a classic white tank with men’s boxers, the first time Hanes has sold them specifically for women.

“In my first meetings with Hanes I spoke about how I always stole my husband’s boxers and wore them out to coffee or to bed, and I begged for them to allow me to use their men’s boxers, and they did,” Paul says.

The collection features 45 products, including fluffy bathrobes, waffle pants, long-sleeve sets, a triangle bralette and boy short two-packs, cami sleep dresses, and the husband-inspired boxers. On theme with the drop, small keychains in the shape of a cow wearing boxers will also be available.

While the silhouettes are classic Hanes, the patterns feature some of Dairy Boy’s most recognizable motifs, including lily of the valley, a brown bear print, camo, plaid, blue and brown pinstripe, and tartan.

The collaboration has been in the works for almost two years, as a silent project that grew alongside the brand’s own successes. Dairy Boy tripled its quarterly orders year over year, surpassing total orders from 2025 in the first nine months of 2026. And those who order seem to come back. In the third quarter of 2026, Dairy Boy reported a year-over-year increase of 312% in repeat costumer volume.

The company has grown, Paul says, thanks to its operations that resemble that of a tech company—integrating technology like AI into their back-end systems and keeping the company team lean. The startup-like structure is paired with Paul’s creative direction, which she says is driven by her gut instinct.

“I am really driving the car here, and if there is no data supporting something, but I really believe in a style, we will order it,” Paul says. “There’s no outside investment, so it’s really easy for us to make decisions quickly.”

Despite being the smaller name in the collaboration, Paul sees the Dairy Boy collection as testament to synergy, pairing the brand’s cultural pull with the infrastructure of legacy companies.

“Target has thousands of stores across America. That is something I don’t have,” she says. “The amount of people that I can get to my website for a drop is something that Target doesn’t have.”

#10610. Android Auto cutting off older devices, now requires Android 11 or newer

Google has officially dropped support for some older Android versions in Android Auto, now requiring Android 11 or newer to function.

On a support page, Google says that Android 11.0 or newer is now required to use Android Auto:

An Android phone with Android 11.0 (Red Velvet Cake) or higher and an active data plan.

Previously, Google supported Android 9 and Android 10 for the in-car experience, a minimum requirement that itself was raised back in 2024 (but not enforced until 2025).

Some drivers started seeing a “Phone will no longer be supported” message in October 2026, but Google only updated its documentation this week. Android Auto 18.1, the latest app update, still supports Android 10.

#10609. Adobe is fully in its agent era

I am a big fan of artificial intelligence taking on the miserable tasks of creative work. Renaming and tagging footage, syncing multiple camera angles, reformatting an ad for 50 different aspect ratios? Let the computer do that, thanks. Adobe showed me how its AI agent can do all that, right inside its apps, back in June. But actual creative work? Pass.

Today, at its Max conference, Adobe is announcing something far more radical than anything it showed me just a few months ago. The company is previewing what it calls local MCP integrations with Creative Cloud tools. MCP is the Model Context Protocol, an open standard Anthropic created in late 2024 that acts as a universal adapter, letting any AI agent plug into any software tool.

The integrations would let third-party agents like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini work directly inside your local Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects projects. On your machine. With access to your layers, vector paths, footage bins, and sequences. The projects stay editable by hand, and users will be able to, in Adobe’s words, “step in at any moment.” The apps themselves need to be installed and licensed on your computer, Adobe tells me, because the agent works locally in your project files with the full depth of the desktop tools.

Adobe’s tools already work with third-party AIs—just the other way around. Since December 2025, ChatGPT users have been able to call on Photoshop, Express, and Acrobat to do design work right in OpenAI’s service. And back in April 2026, Adobe launched a connector for Claude to allow it to use more than 50 tools from Photoshop, Illustrator, or Premiere within the Anthropic AI’s cloud-based service. In September, the same ability came to Google.

In all those cases, you drop a file—a PDF, an image, whatever—into a conversation with the AI, ask it to do things to it, and Adobe’s tools will take care of it. The integration allowed users to continue work later in Adobe’s apps.

The new local MCP integrations flip that around, changing who is in control.

In theory, with Adobe’s own AI agent—now rebranded as Adobe Creative Agent—you know that there’s some degree of control and accountability. Until now, Adobe decided how much its agent could do on its own. With MCP, an outside agent gets the same tools, and Adobe can’t vouch for what it does with them. I don’t know about you, but I feel vertigo. Is this ready, even as a beta? Can we trust these agents with our files? And do we really want to?

It seems that plenty of creators are willing to go further in their use of AI. In the Creators’ Toolkit Report that Adobe released alongside these announcements, a survey of more than 2,000 U.S. creators, 77% say the final creative decision should always remain with the human, even when using agents. They want the help. They want to drive the wheel, too.

But there’s an obvious contradiction between the want and what they get. Some 68% of those using creative AI say they at least sometimes settle for results that don’t fully match their vision. Why? Maybe the answer is that 59% say agents save them time. Or that 36% say agents helped them finish projects that were previously too complex. 

Three altitudes of AI

It’s also happening faster than I could have imagined. Forest Key, Adobe’s VP of Firefly and Agentic AI, told me back in June about what he described as three altitudes of AI. The first is the assistant that strips away drudgery. In an example from that launch we saw an agent in Premiere doing its work: taking a pile of randomly named files, sorting them into bins, renaming and tagging clips using computer vision, syncing footage from three cameras with a separate audio track, and dropping a marker on the timeline wherever an interviewer asked a question.

The second altitude is an AI thought partner, while you keep adding your taste and editorial voice. The third is agents that run full automations while you only check in periodically.

Today, Adobe is also previewing always-on agents, coming first to the Firefly AI Assistant, that take on recurring work in the background—organizing incoming assets, checking quality, preparing content for different channels—while creators set the goal, review the plan, and approve the results. That’s a first step toward altitude three. MCP means agents Adobe didn’t build can climb the same ladder. The local MCP integrations won’t enter beta until early 2027.

Agent as partner

Adobe started its agentic push back in April, when it deployed the Adobe Creative Agent in Firefly, in beta mode. This agent could do the work for you, not just vomit generative AI bitmaps. In June, other Adobe programs also got agentic AI capabilities in beta testing: Premiere, Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign, and Frame.io. That’s when Adobe’s agent started working on your actual projects from inside its apps. After Effects joined the agentic party in September. 

At Adobe Max, the company is adding new capabilities to the Adobe Creative Agent. In Firefly, the assistant can now remember formats, colors, brand guidelines, and characters to apply across projects. A new Plan Mode lets you review, edit, and approve the agent’s plan before it starts, and a model selector lets you pick which AI model does the work. 

The agent is also coming to Premiere mobile in private beta, where it can turn footage into editable first cuts and make edits with plain-language instructions. In desktop Premiere, it can do really complex things, like apply effects across every clip in a sequence, track masked subjects through a frame, and adjust color and exposure across an entire sequence at once.

Until now, there was no official way for outside AI agents to work inside your local projects like Adobe’s agent can. Whenever it becomes available next year, MCP access to Adobe’s apps for agents like Claude or ChatGPT will truly change things. You won’t bring your work to the third-party agent’s home anymore. The third-party agent will come into your home, get its own bedroom, and half of your fridge.

Lingering questions

Having your own ghost artist is a very tempting yet dangerous proposition. What happens if a third-party agent corrupts a sequence, generates something licensing-toxic inside your project, or quietly burns through generative credits? The accountability chain gets blurry fast. 

Anyone could ask Claude to pull reference imagery from the web, then composite it into your project using Photoshop’s own tools to make a document to open and refine yourself. I doubt Adobe’s own assistant will ever do that. First, many of Adobe’s own customers would hate it. And then, imagine the copyright hell that could ensue.

Asked where liability sits between Adobe, the agent provider, and the creator in that scenario, Adobe only pointed back to its answer that MCP is still a preview. When I asked whether third-party agent actions will carry Content Credentials—the provenance standard the company champions—Adobe also told me that it is “working through how provenance will be supported.” As for credit usage, creators will be able to set parameters and review plans before always-on agents run, but on cost Adobe says it is “exploring ways to provide an upfront estimate.”

Those cost questions aren’t only about outside agents, either. Logically, Adobe’s own assistants already burn credits: The After Effects beta started charging them for its AI Assistant on November 6, 2026.

It just feels to me that, for all the good stuff we get from AI helping with work, there’s still a divide when it comes to actual creative work, one that is full of contradictions at many levels. For now, the open questions seem to outnumber the guardrails.

The strategy question

Then there is the matter about what Adobe gains from opening its walled garden to the AI startup hordes. Why give up the last workflow chokepoint it fully owned? 

Maybe they don’t have any options here. Perhaps this is all about the AI agent craze and MCP becoming the standard. Fighting this wave may be seen as worse—especially by greedy stockholders—than riding it. 

What is clear is that the signs of a company-wide pivot to agents are everywhere. A single Adobe Creative Agent now powers the Firefly assistant, the Creative Cloud assistants, and a new private beta in Premiere mobile, while another service called CX Enterprise Coworker in GenStudio orchestrates agents across brands’ content supply chains, according to the company.

“Many creative professionals already use third-party agents that connect to MCP-enabled apps for parts of their production workflow, and they’ve told us they want those agents to work with the tools they trust to finish the job,” Adobe told me in an email. Translation: The customers were already halfway out the door. Let’s keep them in before they find an alternative, integrate it into their workflow, and start canceling subscriptions.

If MCP works as billed, the change will be profound. Your creative software would become a workshop where you hire whichever AI subcontractor you trust—while Adobe repositions itself not as the brain, but as the bench where everyone works. That is either a masterclass in platform strategy or the beginning of Creative Cloud as someone else’s commodity front-end.

Whatever their business strategy is, this new world feels built on shaky grounds. We are climbing the ladder that Key, Adobe’s agentic AI VP, drew for me in June a lot faster than we can build safety checkpoints and best practices rules. #10607. Anthropic stock listing: Target price range hints at valuation lower than rumored reports as IPO date nears

Rumors have spread for months that Anthropic’s IPO valuation could reach the head-spinning sum of $2 trillion. 

In reality, the creator of Claude is looking at a valuation range of $1 trillion to $1.4 trillion, according to a range of analyses. 

On Tuesday, Anthropic’s updated Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing provided the clearest look yet at what its IPO will look like. 

The AI company plans to offer 825 million shares of Class A common stock at an estimated price of $70 to $78 each. Anthropic is selling more than 801 million shares, while its selling stockholders are offering another 23.6 million shares.

Anthropic is also offering up Class N common stock in a private placement to Google, Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Broadcom, Micron Technology, Microsoft, and TSMC Partners.

Google and Nvidia will purchase the largest amount at 135,135,135 shares each, worth about $10 million. 

Anthropic predicts the private placement deal will be worth about $26 billion. In total, Anthropic could raise up to $64.35 billion through the IPO. 

The exact date of the Anthropic IPO is still up in the air but likely to be mid-November. The company has applied for listing on Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT.” 

How is Anthropic doing? 

It’s no secret that investors are continuing to fear an AI bubble—with the midterm election results offering more uncertainty about the future of data center buildouts.

Anthropic has seen its growth slow this year. In October, the company reported a 45% increase in revenue for quarter three, down from 60% between quarters one and two.

Following these results, investors had started leaning toward an IPO valuation closer to $1.5 trillion, rather than $2 trillion.

Of course, an IPO valuation over $1 trillion is still remarkable. If accurate, Anthropic will have one of the biggest IPOs of all time—though falling short of SpaceX’s record $1.77 trillion listing earlier this year.

#10606. Meta’s Horizon+ looks to become Meta VR+ and include 3D movies

Meta Horizon+ is rumored to be changing its name to Meta VR+ and may start including movies in addition to games with the subscription price.

Meta’s quest (ahem) to distance itself from the Horizon era is in full swing, and the latest rumor says it’s time for the company’s Game Pass-like subscription to change its brand name. VR leaker Nori posted a screenshot on X showing a handful of 3D movies coming to the Meta VR Plus service. Considering there is no such Meta VR Plus service currently, the obvious conclusion is that Meta Horizon+ is being renamed once again.

Meta Horizon+ currently includes over 100 games with its $7.99 per month subscription and is similar to Microsoft’s Xbox Game Pass service in many ways. Unironically, Meta Horizon+ also includes the basic Xbox Game Pass tier with over 50 Xbox games playable via the Game Pass cloud. Meta offers a 3-month trial with every new Meta Quest purchase.

The new Meta VR+ service is purported to include 3D movies as well, although we don’t yet know if this will be included in the regular $7.99 per month rate, or if Meta will be introducing additional content tiers, as services like Netflix, Disney+, Xbox Game Pass, and others do. Based on the screenshot, these will be big-name movies and are likely positioned to enhance the value of the upcoming $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, although all the same content will work on existing Meta Quest 3 units.

Meta has been slowly distancing itself from the “Horizon” name ever since the beginning of this year, when its VR division got a big reset. In a February blog post, Samantha Ryan, the VP of Content at Meta’s Reality Labs, spoke about the changes to the company’s strategy, including the loss of most in-house VR gaming studios. Since then, several prominent VR developers from Meta have gone on to create independent studios, including the super-popular Supernatural exercise app.

Meta then decoupled the unpopular Horizon Metaverse from its headsets, moving it to mobile-only, and has been removing the “Horizon” name from just about everything since then. Meta Horizon+ looks to be the latest big change, as the company moves toward “Meta VR” branding, which is clearer and separates its VR division from mobile and smart glasses efforts.

#10605. Top 6 AI Image Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A designer who once spent an afternoon searching stock libraries can now describe the picture they want and have four versions in under a minute. AI image generators have moved from curiosity to everyday tool for blog headers, product mockups, ad concepts, game art and slide decks. The quality gap between tools has narrowed, but the differences that remain matter a lot: how well each follows a detailed prompt, whether it can render readable text, how it handles edits, and what you are allowed to do with the result.

This guide compares six of the best-known options, what each does well and where each falls short. Models, plans and limits change often, so check each vendor's own pages before you commit to a workflow.

OpenArt’s AI image generator puts several image models behind one interface. Its generator page lists models including GPT Image 2.5, Grok Imagine, Qwen Image 3, Nano Banana 2 and Seedream 5.0 Pro, and lets you create images from text prompts or reference photos. It also lists tools for camera angle control, upscaling, collages and a Character Builder for keeping characters consistent across scenes, with 4K export.

Best for: Creators who want to compare several models on the same prompt without juggling separate subscriptions and accounts.

Limitations: The page offers a free start but does not state credit amounts or plan details, and it does not address commercial use, so check the pricing and licensing pages before using results for client work. Output quality depends on which model you pick.

OpenAI's image generation in ChatGPT works inside the chat interface, which makes iteration natural: generate an image, then ask for changes in plain language. OpenAI highlights accurate text rendering, the ability to follow prompts with many distinct objects, and consistent characters across multi-turn edits. You can also upload reference images and have the model transform them. It handles both photorealistic and stylized looks.

Best for: Marketers and writers who want to describe, refine and re-describe an image without learning a new tool.

Limitations: OpenAI notes that tall images such as posters can be cropped too tightly, and that dense small text, multilingual text and precise graphs can still go wrong. Images can take up to a minute to render. All generated images carry C2PA metadata identifying their source.

Gemini's image generation runs on Google's Nano Banana models. Google highlights character consistency, text rendering in many languages, combining several photos, precise editing and 2K resolution. A free tier covers image generation and editing, while the most advanced model requires a Google AI plan. You start from the "Create images" option in the Gemini app, then prompt or upload a picture to edit.

Best for: People who need to keep the same subject across several images, or who want to edit existing photos quickly.

Limitations: Usage limits apply, and the strongest model is behind a paid plan. Images include an invisible SynthID watermark and a visible AI label, which is good for transparency but may not suit every use.

Midjourney is an independent research lab known for images with a strong, painterly look. Its official site points users to a sign-up flow and to a Discord community and help center for support. Many creators choose it for concept art, mood boards and illustration where style matters more than literal accuracy.

Best for: Artists, art directors and game designers who want rich, stylized results and enjoy exploring variations.

Limitations: I could not confirm current pricing, trial terms or feature details from Midjourney's public pages, so check them yourself before subscribing. The workflow can feel less like a normal app than the others on this list, and it is not the easiest route for precise, text-heavy graphics.

Adobe Firefly is built for professionals who already work in Creative Cloud. Adobe states that its Firefly models are commercially safe, trained on licensed Adobe Stock and public domain content, and outputs carry Content Credentials that show AI involvement. It offers text-to-image, image-to-image, sketch-to-image and style transfer, plus editing tools such as background removal, object removal, upscaling and generative expand. It connects with Photoshop, Illustrator, Lightroom and Adobe Express, and also lets you use partner models from other companies.

Best for: Designers and brand teams who need clear licensing and want AI inside the apps they already use.

Limitations: Plans work on a credit system, so heavy use adds up. Adobe lists a free tier with limited daily generations and paid plans starting at about $9.99 a month, but confirm current terms on its site.

Ideogram built its reputation on a problem that trips up many generators: readable text. Its current models are presented as producing clean typography in different layouts, with attention to prompt fidelity and reliable editing. It also offers an API with access to a catalog of models, and has released open weights for one earlier model for local use and customization under its license.

Best for: Posters, social graphics, logo concepts and anything where words are part of the image.

Limitations: The pages I checked did not describe a free plan, so look at current plans before relying on it. Like every generator, it still needs a human to proofread the text it produces.

Start with the job. If you want to compare several models side by side, try OpenArt. If you want to talk your way to a finished image, try ChatGPT or Gemini. If you need images that will sit inside a branded design workflow, Firefly is the safer fit. If you are chasing a distinctive look, Midjourney deserves a trial. If text must be perfect, test Ideogram.

Run the same prompt in two or three tools before paying. Differences in composition, hands, faces and text show up quickly, and they matter more than any feature list.

Reviews only go so far, because your own use case is what counts. Pick one realistic job, for example a 16:9 header image for a blog post about web performance, and run the same prompt through two or three tools. Write the prompt once and paste it unchanged, so the comparison is fair:

Then score each result on five questions: Did it follow every instruction? Are there odd details in hands, edges or objects? Is any text spelled correctly? Does it still look good when cropped to a square? Could you license it for your project? Ten minutes of this teaches more than any feature list, and it shows how much editing each tool needs before you can publish.

Most readers of this guide will put these images on web pages, where a few habits matter more than the generator you choose.

There is no single best AI image generator. The right pick depends on whether you value conversation, style, licensing, control or typography. Test two or three on a real project, compare the output, and keep a human in charge of the final choice. Whatever you generate, review it for errors and label AI-made images clearly where your audience would expect it.

Are AI-generated images free to use commercially? It depends on the provider and your plan. Read the licensing terms for the tool you use, and consider vendors that publish how their models were trained if you work for clients.

Which AI image generator is best for text in images? Ideogram and ChatGPT both highlight text rendering, and Gemini lists it as a feature. Test each with your own wording and proofread the result.

Do AI images have watermarks? Some do. OpenAI adds C2PA metadata, Google adds an invisible SynthID watermark and a visible label, and Adobe attaches Content Credentials.

Can I use more than one image model without separate accounts? Yes. Platforms such as OpenArt put several models in one interface, which makes side-by-side testing easier. Check the licensing terms for each model you use.

Should I add alt text to AI-generated images? Yes, when the image carries meaning. Describe what it shows or why it is there. Purely decorative images can use an empty alt attribute, following the W3C guidance.

South Korean chip startup DEEPX says its new AI chip will be at the heart of upcoming Hyundai robots.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Processors generating excess heat play a significant part in contemporary data center design, cost, and resource use. However, things could be vastly different if AI chips were more efficient and ran far cooler. South Korean chip startup DEEPX, recently featured by CNBC, thinks its AI chip designs are the answer. DEEPX demonstrated its DX-M1 processor’s cool-running capabilities in a bizarre new dairy-based thermal benchmark. While rival chips caused a knob of butter to sizzle in seconds, atop the DEEPX solution, the butter block remains solid.

Concerns over AI data center proliferation are growing worldwide. These developments are shaping business, the environment, and politics. Some people have very strong feelings about them, and hundreds of people have risked being thrown into jail protesting data centers. The CNBC report linked in the intro looks into why modern data centers are problematic, and indicates that the core issues stem from the use of hot-running processors and the extensive power and cooling apparatus they need.

DEEPX says its simple answer is to “make the AI chips themselves run cooler.” The CNBC video includes a demo of the ultra-low-power DX-M1 processor. In a side-by-side test against unnamed rival AI chips, you can see the DX-M1 NPU is clearly cooler. DEEPX CEO Kim Nok-won claims a temperature difference of 25 to more than 40 degrees Celsius compared with competitors. Kim said the side-by-side chips processed “the same AI workload… and every chip melted the butter except the last chip [DX-M1].”

The dairy-based thermal challenge is certainly eyebrow-raising, but we note some big gaps in the comparison information. Most notable was the question of how fast each processor tackles the test workload. Anyone can run a chip cool if the power and clocks are scaled back. PC enthusiasts undervolt and/or underclock their GPUs all the time for efficiency, better thermals, and reduced fan noise.

DEEPX’s DX-M1 NPU has been produced on Samsung 5nm since August 2025, according to The Elec reports. It has won approximately $13.3M worth of orders thanks to this sliver of silicon. The company is planning to move forward with the next-gen DX-M2 AI chip, which is based on Samsung 2nm, with its mass production aiming for H2 2027.

In conclusion, these NPUs look set for edge computing and robotics applications, so they aren’t really competing in the same space as the racks of power-gulping Nvidia Blackwell and Ruben GPUs featured in the CNBC news feature. Eventually, we might see the hundreds or thousands of hot-running Nvidia GPUs with beefy liquid cooling apparatus get replaced by cooler-running custom accelerators. Such an innovation could cool the backlash against AI data centers. However, DEEPX’s DX-M1 or even DX-M2 chips aren’t going to compete in that space, so this butter test is a bit of a red herring.

The CNBC report also highlights SK hynix’s work on iHBM, a next-gen low-power consumption, and cool-running. The ‘i’ stands for ‘Integrated Cooling Element,’ according to an exec talking to CNBC. CoolIT is also trying a similar approach by bringing water cooling even closer to the heat-generating silicon.
